title: Effect of daylight exposure on sustained attention in open-plan offices: a randomized crossover study
abstract: This randomized crossover trial examined sustained attention performance among 48 knowledge workers in an open-plan office across three lighting conditions: natural daylight only, supplemented electric light, and electric light only. Sustained attention was assessed with the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) at 2-hour intervals. Workers exposed to natural daylight ≥150 lux at the workplane showed significantly lower lapse rates (M=4.1 vs 7.8 per session, p<.001) compared to the electric-only condition, controlling for time-of-day and circadian phase. Effects were strongest in the 10:00–14:00 window and diminished after 15:00.

title: Daylighting quality metrics and worker cognitive performance: a longitudinal field study
abstract: We followed 120 knowledge workers across six open-plan offices for nine months, correlating continuous illuminance monitoring with weekly cognitive assessments. Spatial daylight autonomy above 50% was associated with 12% faster performance on executive function tasks and 8% fewer self-reported attentional failures. Mixed-effects models confirmed daylight as a significant predictor after controlling for thermal comfort, noise levels, and desk location. The circadian-disruption pathway was partially mediated by evening melatonin suppression measured via actigraphy sub-sample.

title: Biophilic classroom design and student cognitive engagement: a quasi-experimental study in higher education
abstract: A quasi-experimental design compared two university classrooms differing only in biophilic elements (living wall, natural materials, plant arrangements) while controlling for acoustic conditions and thermal comfort. Cognitive engagement was measured using NASA-TLX, Stroop task performance, and continuous EEG alpha/theta ratio. Students in the biophilic classroom showed significantly lower perceived mental workload (p=.009) and 14% improvement on Stroop interference scores. Acoustic noise was monitored and did not differ significantly between conditions. Results support biophilic design as an independent predictor of classroom cognitive performance.

title: The effect of correlated colour temperature on reading fluency in secondary classrooms
abstract: Forty-two secondary school students (ages 13–15) were tested under three CCT conditions (2700 K, 4000 K, 6500 K) in a counterbalanced within-subjects design. Reading fluency speed and working memory (digit-span and n-back) were measured after 30-minute adaptation periods. Results showed a significant CCT × task interaction (F(4,164)=6.3, p<.001): 4000 K produced the fastest reading fluency, while 6500 K supported best n-back performance. Thermal environment was maintained at 22 ± 0.5 °C. Findings suggest CCT recommendations should be task-differentiated rather than uniform.

title: Window-to-floor ratio and glare probability in knowledge-worker offices: a Monte Carlo simulation study
abstract: Using Radiance-based Monte Carlo simulations across 240 virtual office configurations, we modelled the relationship between window-to-floor ratio (WFR) and annualised Daylight Glare Probability (DGP) for four orientations. Results show an asymptotic DGP curve: WFR >35% on south-facing façades produces DGP >0.35 (intolerable glare) for >15% of occupied hours without shading. The cognitive alertness proxy (vertical illuminance at eye level 350 lux) is achievable at WFR 25–30% with appropriately designed shading. Façade orientation moderates the optimal WFR by ±8 percentage points.

title: Indoor plants and cognitive restoration in office workers: a preregistered field experiment
abstract: We conducted a preregistered 8-week field experiment with 96 office workers randomly assigned to three plant density conditions (0, 1, or 4 plants per 10m²). Attentional restoration was measured weekly using the Attention Network Test (ANT) and salivary cortisol. High plant density produced significantly greater alerting network efficiency (p=.012) and lower afternoon cortisol (p=.028) versus the control condition. Maintenance events (watering, replacement) were logged and modelled as covariates; their disruption effect was non-significant. Results support a causal dose-response relationship between plant density and attentional restoration.

title: Dynamic lighting and cognitive fatigue in hospital nursing staff
abstract: This 12-week parallel-group trial assessed whether circadian-tuned dynamic lighting reduced cognitive fatigue in night-shift nurses. Forty nurses were assigned to static 3000 K lighting or dynamic lighting shifting from 6500 K (20:00–00:00) to 2700 K (01:00–07:00). The Samn–Perelli fatigue scale and N-back performance were measured at shift start, midpoint, and end. Dynamic lighting reduced end-of-shift fatigue scores by 1.4 points (95% CI 0.7–2.1, p<.001) and improved N-back accuracy by 6% (p=.018). Habituation was assessed via longitudinal mixed-effects and was not a significant moderator after 4 weeks.

title: Outdoor view content and attentional restoration in home-office workers during COVID-19 lockdown
abstract: A cross-sectional survey of 1,247 remote workers captured view content (nature, urban, obstructed), view distance (estimated in meters), window size, and scores on the Attentional Function Index (AFI) and Perceived Restorativeness Scale (PRS). Regression analysis found that nature-content views predicted significantly higher AFI (β=0.31, p<.001) and PRS (β=0.28, p<.001) after controlling for view distance, window size, residential density, and number of plants. Obstructed views were negatively associated with restorativeness. Results strengthen the view-from-window literature and extend it to the remote work context.

title: Thermal preference and cognitive comfort in mixed-mode buildings: seasonal acclimatisation effects
abstract: Occupants in three mixed-mode university buildings completed bi-weekly thermal comfort surveys and cognitive performance batteries (n=210 person-surveys over 14 months). Mixed-effects models showed that self-reported thermal preference alignment with actual operative temperature predicted higher scores on working memory and processing speed tasks (r=0.29, p<.001). Seasonal acclimatisation was modelled as a continuous covariate; its effect was significant in summer but not winter, suggesting that cognitive comfort benefits of thermal preference control are most pronounced during periods of high ambient temperature variability.

title: Reverberation time and reading comprehension in open-plan primary classrooms
abstract: Forty-eight Grade 2 and Grade 4 classrooms across 12 schools were acoustically measured (RT60) and matched with end-of-year standardized reading and mathematics scores (n=1,156 students). Multi-level regression controlling for teacher experience, socioeconomic status, and class size found that RT60 above 0.6 s was associated with a 6.3 percentile-point decrease in reading scores (p=.003) but not mathematics. Background noise level (dB LAeq) was a partial mediator. Results suggest a reading-specific sensitivity to classroom reverberation, with RT60 ≤ 0.4 s as the evidence-supported target for early literacy.

title: Green roofs and occupant well-being: a controlled pre-post study in urban residential towers
abstract: Residents of two matched urban residential towers — one retrofitted with a green roof and rooftop garden access, one unchanged — completed measures of perceived stress (PSS-10), cognitive restoration (Kaplan BRS), and life satisfaction at baseline and 6-month follow-up. The intervention group showed significantly lower PSS-10 scores at follow-up (Δ=-2.8, 95% CI -4.1 to -1.5, p<.001). Building energy models confirmed that the green roof reduced indoor summer temperatures by 1.2 °C; this thermal effect was included as a covariate and did not account for the full stress-reduction benefit, suggesting an independent restorative pathway.

title: Validation of daylighting simulation against post-occupancy illuminance measurements
abstract: We compared Radiance/EnergyPlus simulation outputs against 18 months of continuous illuminance sensor data from a LEED-certified office building (n=42 sensor locations). Simulation underestimated workplane illuminance by a mean of 18% (95% CI 11–25%), with largest errors in south-facing perimeter zones during winter. Occupant blind usage, not captured in the standard simulation workflow, explained 63% of the variance in prediction error. Self-reported cognitive alertness correlated more strongly with measured illuminance (r=0.41) than simulated illuminance (r=0.24), highlighting the occupant-behaviour gap in current simulation-to-cognition pipelines.

title: Personal lighting control and mood in shared offices: a peer-norm mediation study
abstract: An online vignette experiment (n=384 office workers) manipulated personal lighting control availability and peer lighting norms (cooperative vs. competitive norm). Personal control improved mood and perceived cognitive performance when peer norms were cooperative, but not when norms were competitive (interaction β=0.22, p=.004). A follow-up field study (n=88) in two open-plan offices partially replicated the interaction using ecological momentary assessment. Results suggest that the cognitive and affective benefits of personal lighting control are contingent on shared social context and cannot be extrapolated from single-occupant experiments.

title: Spatial daylight autonomy in LEED-certified schools: a cross-validation against cognitive outcomes
abstract: A review of 22 LEED-certified schools (2015–2021) examined whether classrooms meeting the sDA300/50% threshold also showed better cognitive outcomes in post-occupancy evaluations. Cognitive outcomes were available for 14 schools via standardized test score datasets. A mixed-methods regression found no significant correlation between sDA compliance and reading or math scores (r=0.12, p=.67). Schools with high sDA but misaligned occupancy schedules (certification rated 8am-6pm; actual 7:30am-4:30pm) systematically underperformed, supporting the temporal-mismatch hypothesis. Findings raise questions about sDA's validity as a cognitive-performance predictor.

title: Melanopsin activation, chronotype, and error rates in night-shift industrial workers
abstract: Thirty industrial night-shift workers were genotyped for PER3 VNTR chronotype polymorphism and monitored with spectral radiance sensors (melanopic EDI) at workstations over 6-week periods. Neuropsychological assessments (Trail Making Test, PVT) were administered at shift midpoint. Higher melanopic EDI (>100 lux eq.) predicted lower TMT-B time (β=-4.8 s, p=.022) and fewer PVT lapses (β=-1.2, p=.041), but effects were moderated by chronotype: M-type workers benefited less than E-type workers. Sleep debt (actigraphy-measured) attenuated but did not eliminate the melanopsin effect, suggesting a separable contribution of spectral composition beyond sleep opportunity.

title: Energy policy impacts on occupant visual comfort: beyond thermal and electrical metrics
abstract: This paper reviews energy policy frameworks and their alignment with occupant visual comfort standards. The authors argue that current energy codes prioritise power density (W/m²) over spectral and temporal quality metrics that drive cognitive alertness. A framework is proposed integrating melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (mEDI) into energy codes. The paper does not include new empirical data on cognitive outcomes but provides a policy rationale grounded in existing circadian literature.

title: Horticultural therapy and elderly cognitive rehabilitation: a systematic review
abstract: A systematic review of 14 randomised controlled trials examined whether horticultural therapy programmes improved cognitive function in older adults with mild cognitive impairment. Results were heterogeneous; only 4 of 14 studies reported significant MMSE improvements. The review is limited to elderly clinical populations in structured therapy settings and does not examine the effects of passive plant presence on healthy adult cognition in workplace settings. Evidence quality was rated low-to-moderate (GRADE).
